To demonstrate, let's consider the following ratio:

$$
2:6
$$

If we multiply *both* numbers by $5,$ for example, we get the ratio $10:30.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,2 &  & : & \,\,\, & \,\,6 &  \\ \,\,↓\times \,5 &  &  &  & \,\,↓\times \,5 &  \\ \,10 &  & : &  & \,30 & \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ratios $2:6$ and $10:30$ are equivalent. 

Similarly, if we take the ratio $2:6$ and divide *both* numbers by $2,$ we get $1:3.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,2 &  & : & \,\,\, & \,\,6 &  \\ \,\,↓÷\,2 &  &  &  & \,\,↓÷\,2 &  \\ \,\,1 &  & : &  & \,\,3 & \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ratios  $2:6$ and  $1:3$ are also equivalent." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186075035 :tutorial/content "Suppose that the following two ratios are equivalent:

![](images/c6/c673bfcd099ef612f48bd0da7f8535cb9406d23088392e056884fb9415bb5100.svg)

In this case, we need to get $12$ from ${\color{blue}{3}},$ so we multiply ${\color{blue}{3}}$ by $4.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,3 &  & : & \,\,\, & \,\,5 &  \\ \,\,↓\times \,4 &  &  &  & \,\,↓\times \,4 &  \\ 12 &  & : &  & \,\boxed{\text{[math]\phantom{0}[/math]}} & \end{aligned}
$$

So, to get ![](images/50/50f3c1b8dc3b1628130d1de11abcc455fc22006f32b7486f658c8134fcc3221c.svg) from ${\color{red}{5}},$ we multiply ${\color{red}{5}}$ by $4$ as well: 

$$
{\color{red}5} \times 4 = \bbox[3px,lightgray]{\color{red}20}
$$

Therefore, the missing number is $20.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186075036 :tutorial/content "We can simplify ratios by dividing both numbers in the ratio by a common factor.

To demonstrate, let's simplify the following ratio: 

$$
18:9
$$

The numbers $18$ and $9$ share a common factor of $9,$ so we can divide both numbers by $9$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,18 &  & : & \,\,\,\, & \,\,\,9 &  \\ \,\,↓÷\,\,9 &  &  &  & \,\,\,↓÷\,\,9 &  \\ \,\,2 &  & : &  & \,\,\,1 & \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $18:9$ is equivalent to $2:1.$
